p: The Hebrew has Darius the Mede. Both Greek versions read "Cyrus."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QDan-c (4Q114, dated to the late second century BC as reported by its editors), where the word is preserved
Theodotion and the Old Greek (Codex Chisianus, in Swete's edition)

why: The Hebrew is the older witness and matches 9:1 and 5:31. The Greek reading smooths the well-known problem of who Darius the Mede was, and 10:1 puts the vision in Cyrus' third year.
b: Both Greek traditions read "the first year of Cyrus." The Greek translators may have had a different Hebrew text or changed it on purpose. Darius the Mede is not known outside Daniel; see the notes at 5:31 and 9:1 for the views (Gubaru, Cyrus himself, Astyages, Darius I).

p: The Masoretic Text has a noun, "my standing." A Qumran copy and Theodotion have a verb, "I stood." The Old Greek has a different sentence.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
4QDan-c (4Q114), where the word is preserved (Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription); Theodotion (estên, "I stood")
The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus): "he said to me to be strong and take courage"
readings.en: he said to me to be strong and to be brave
readings.plain: he told me to be strong and brave

why: The Masoretic noun makes sense with the verb understood, and the Plain's "I was standing" gives the sense of the noun and the verb alike. Two witnesses, the scroll and Theodotion, read the verb. The Old Greek's sentence is a different text.
b: The speaker is the heavenly messenger of chapter 10. The scroll and Theodotion agree on "I stood," and the meaning is the same as the Masoretic Text's; the Plain needs no change.

p: The Hebrew letters can be read "his arm" or "his seed." Theodotion reads "seed."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, pointed zero'o "his arm" (so also the Old Greek, Codex Chisianus: "his arm")
Theodotion (Greek: "his seed"); the consonants זרעו can also be read zar'o

why: The pointed Hebrew is the base text, and "arm" repeats the "strength of the arm" just before it.
b: Those who read "seed" think of the baby son of Berenice, murdered with her. Both readings fit the story.

t: "The one who fathered her" or "the girl"?
p: The same letters can read as a father or a young woman. Theodotion has "the girl."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, pointed hayyoldah "the one begetting her"
readings.en: and the one who fathered her

readings.w: Theodotion (Greek: "the young woman"), reading hayaldah

why: The pointed Hebrew is the base text. The unpointed letters allow "the girl" (hayaldah), which would mean Berenice's attendant or child; a father fits because he is named between those who brought her and those who backed her.

p: The written text (Ketiv) has "his son." The reading tradition (Qere) has "his sons."

readings.w: Qere of the Masoretic Text; Theodotion (Greek: "his sons")
Ketiv of the Masoretic Text; the Old Greek (Codex Chisianus: "his son")

why: The Masoretes read "sons" aloud. The rest of the verse switches between plural and singular verbs, which both readings explain. Two brothers (Seleucus III and Antiochus III) fit the plural; the singular fits Antiochus III alone.

a: Men of violence from your own people
p: Theodotion has "the sons of the rest of your people." The Old Greek has a different sentence about rebuilding and prophecy.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; 4QDan-a (4Q112) and 4QDan-c (4Q114), where the words are preserved
readings.en: and the sons of the violent ones of your people
readings.plain: Men of violence from your own people

readings.w: Theodotion (Greek: "the sons of the rest of your people")
readings.orig: οἱ υἱοὶ τῶν λοιπῶν τοῦ λαοῦ σου
readings.en: the sons of the rest of your people
readings.plain: the sons of the rest of your people

readings.w: The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus): "he will rebuild the fallen parts of your nation, and will rise up to raise up the prophecy, and they will stumble"
readings.orig: ἀνοικοδομήσει τὰ πεπτωκότα τοῦ ἔθνους σου
readings.en: he will rebuild what has fallen of your nation
readings.plain: he will rebuild what has fallen of your nation

why: The Hebrew is the base text, and both scrolls agree with it where they are preserved. Theodotion reads the Hebrew word for "violent" as another word; the Old Greek is a free rewording of the whole line.

a: The one who comes against him
p: The Hebrew is a participle with "against him." Both Greek versions and one Qumran copy agree; the other Qumran copy has a different first letter in the transcription.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; 4QDan-a (4Q112), where the words are preserved; Theodotion (ho eisporeuomenos pros auton) and the Old Greek (Codex Chisianus: ho eisporeuomenos ep' auton)
readings.en: the one who comes to him (against him)
readings.plain: The one who comes against him

readings.w: 4QDan-c (4Q114), as the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription reads the first word (a mem where the Masoretic Text has a bet)

why: Three witnesses agree with the Masoretic Text, and the transcribed form gives no usable word. The Plain keeps "the one who comes against him," with the hostile "against."

a: destruction will be in his hand
p: One Qumran copy has "in his strength." The Masoretic Text, Theodotion and the Old Greek have "hand."

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Theodotion (en tê cheiri autou) and the Old Greek (en tais chersin autou), which read the verb as "be finished" and not "destruction"
readings.plain: destruction will be in his hand

readings.w: 4QDan-c (4Q114), as the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription reads it
readings.plain: destruction will be in his strength

why: Both Greek versions and the Masoretic Text agree on "hand," and the scroll stands alone. "Hand" also matches "in his hand" in 11:11. The Greek translators read the Hebrew kalah as "be completed" ("it will be completed in his hand"), which is a second small difference.

t: "A daughter of the women" or "a daughter of men"?
p: The Hebrew has an odd phrase. One Qumran copy has "men" and the Old Greek has "a daughter of a man."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Theodotion ("a daughter of women")
readings.en: and the daughter of the women

readings.w: 4QDan-c (4Q114), as the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription reads it (the word for "men" is preserved; the word "daughter" before it is restored by the editors); the Old Greek (Codex Chisianus: "a daughter of a man")

why: The Hebrew text is the base. "The women" is hard, and "men" may be a simplification, but two independent witnesses have it. The Plain's "young woman" renders the Hebrew idiom.
b: In 4Q114 the preserved word is 'anashim, "men," where the Masoretic Text has hannashim, "the women." The difference is a single letter.

p: The Old Greek translates the name: "Romans." So does Jerome's Latin.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Theodotion (Kitioi)
The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus: "Romans"); Jerome's Latin Vulgate (Romani)

why: The Hebrew is the base text. The Old Greek and the Latin show how an early translator read "Kittim": as Rome, whose fleet is what the verse describes.

p: Theodotion has "the sanctuary of power." The Old Greek has "the holy place of fear."

readings.w: Masoretic Text
Theodotion: to hagiasma tes dynasteias
The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus): to hagion tou phobou

why: The Hebrew is the base text. Theodotion reads ma'oz as "power," and the Old Greek seems to read the word as "fear" (a possible mix-up of letters or a guess).

t: Three Greek wordings of "the abomination that desolates"
p: The Old Greek has "an abomination of desolation." Theodotion has "a vanished abomination."

readings.w: Masoretic Text
The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus): bdelygma erêmôseôs, the wording that Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14 quote, adding the article
Theodotion: bdelygma êphanismenon (from aphanizô, "make disappear, destroy")
readings.plain: an abomination that has been made to vanish

why: The Hebrew is the base text. The Old Greek follows it word for word. Theodotion changes the sense of the participle: where 12:11 in Theodotion has "an abomination of desolation," 11:31 has a different word.

t: Michael the prince or the angel?
p: Theodotion and the Hebrew say "prince." The Old Greek says "angel."

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Theodotion (Greek archon, "ruler, prince")
The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus: angelos, "angel")

why: The Hebrew sar matches 10:13, 21. The Old Greek says what the "prince" is.
b: In the same verse the Old Greek says the people will be "exalted" instead of "escape," and Theodotion says "be saved."

a: and some to shame, to a horror without end
p: The Old Greek has three groups at the resurrection. The Hebrew and Theodotion have two.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Theodotion ("some to life, some to reproach and everlasting shame")
readings.en: and these to reproaches, to everlasting abhorrence
readings.plain: and some to shame, to a horror without end

readings.w: The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus): some to life, some to reproach, some to scattering and everlasting shame
readings.orig: οἱ δὲ εἰς ὀνειδισμόν, οἱ δὲ εἰς διασπορὰν καὶ αἰσχύνην αἰώνιον
readings.en: some to reproach, some to scattering and everlasting shame
readings.plain: and some to reproach, and some to scattering and shame without end

why: The Hebrew is the base text, and Theodotion agrees with it. The Old Greek's third group looks like an interpretation.

t: "Dust of the ground," "mound of earth" or "breadth of the earth"?
p: The Old Greek says the dead sleep "in the breadth of the earth." Theodotion says "in a mound of earth."

readings.w: Masoretic Text
Theodotion: en gês chômati
The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus): en tô platei tês gês
readings.en: in the breadth (wide surface) of the earth

why: The Hebrew is the base text and echoes Genesis 3:19. The Old Greek's phrase is a free rendering that drops the word "dust." Theodotion's word can mean a grave mound.

a: put the many in the right
t: "Put the many in the right" or "strengthen my words"?
p: The Old Greek has a different second line: "those who strengthen my words."

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.en: and those who justify the many
readings.plain: put the many in the right

readings.w: The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus): "those who make my words strong"

why: The Hebrew is the base text and echoes Isaiah 53:11. Theodotion has an odd text ("and from the righteous of the many"), which may be a corruption or a different reading of the same Hebrew.

a: Many will rove around, and knowledge will multiply
p: The Greek versions read the end of 12:4 very differently.

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.en: many will roam about and knowledge will increase
readings.plain: Many will rove around, and knowledge will multiply

readings.w: Theodotion: "until many are taught and knowledge is multiplied"
readings.orig: ἕως διδαχθῶσιν πολλοὶ καὶ πληθυνθῇ ἡ γνῶσις
readings.en: until many are taught, and knowledge is increased
readings.plain: Many will be taught, and knowledge will multiply

readings.w: The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus): "until the many go mad and the earth is full of injustice"
readings.orig: ἕως ἂν ἀπομανῶσιν οἱ πολλοὶ καὶ πλησθῇ ἡ γῆ ἀδικίας
readings.en: until the many go mad and the earth is filled with injustice
readings.plain: Many will go mad, and the earth will be full of injustice

why: The Hebrew is the base text. Theodotion paraphrases the same Hebrew with a different sense for the first verb; the Old Greek may read ra'ah "evil" for da'at "knowledge."

a: the smashing of the holy people's strength
p: The Hebrew word for "smash" is rendered "scatter" by Theodotion and "release" by the Old Greek.

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.en: the smashing of the hand of the holy people
readings.plain: the smashing of the holy people's strength

readings.w: Theodotion: "when the scattering is completed"
readings.plain: the scattering of the holy people

readings.w: The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus): "the completion of the release of the hands of the holy people"
readings.orig: ἡ συντέλεια χειρῶν ἀφέσεως λαοῦ ἁγίου
readings.en: the finishing of the release of the holy people's hands
readings.plain: the release of the holy people's hands

why: The Hebrew nafats is "shatter" (compare Jeremiah 51:20-23) and fits the persecution. The Greek words read the same letters with a different sense.

p: Theodotion has "from the time of the change of the regular offering." The Old Greek says "stops."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (husar, "was removed")
Theodotion: "from the time of the changing of the continual offering"
readings.en: of the changing of the regular offering

readings.w: The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus): "from when the sacrifice stands away"

why: The Hebrew is the base text and matches 8:11 and 11:31. All three give the same number, 1,290.

p: The Hebrew and Theodotion say "lot." The Old Greek says "glory," and adds "hours."

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Theodotion (kleros, "lot")
The Old Greek (Codex Chisianus): "to your glory," with "days and hours" earlier in the verse

why: The Hebrew goral is the base text. The Old Greek's "glory" fits 12:3, where the faithful shine.
